name: Cairo
tagline: Pyramids, the Nile and a thousand years of empire.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: Come in the cool months, October to March, for the Pyramids and the Nile; catch the Abu Simbel Sun Festival on February 22 or October 22, and avoid the fierce June-to-August desert heat.

ourTake.lede: Cairo rewards patience and an early alarm. See the Pyramids at Giza the moment the site opens, before the heat and the crowds, and give a full unhurried half-day to the Grand Egyptian Museum, which finally does the collection justice. Don't try to cram Islamic Cairo, the Egyptian Museum and Giza into one day; the city is dense and the traffic is real, so slow down and let a good fixer smooth the edges.
ourTake.comeIf: You want the Pyramids, the new Grand Egyptian Museum and a Nile-led week of deep history.
ourTake.skipIf: You need calm, orderly streets or a pure relaxation trip; Cairo is dense and chaotic.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Cairo at Nile Plaza
items.description: The surest hands in the city, a Nile-front tower where nothing is left to chance.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Cairo at the First Residence
items.area: Giza (Nile-side, near the zoo & botanical gardens)
items.description: A stately, residential Four Seasons above the First Mall, grand, calm and quietly grown-up.

items.name: Marriott Mena House, Cairo
credentials: Travel + Leisure World's Best, top MENA city hotels
items.description: The pyramids filling your window from forty acres of gardens, the most storied address in Egypt.

items.name: The St. Regis Cairo
items.description: Butler service and gilded Nile-front glamour, the maison's Egyptian flagship.

items.name: The Nile Ritz-Carlton, Cairo
items.description: A polished Ritz-Carlton on the Nile, steps from Tahrir and the old Egyptian Museum.

items.name: Sofitel Cairo Nile El Gezirah
items.description: An island tower ringed by the Nile on three sides, French art de vivre with the river at every window.

items.name: Kempinski Nile Hotel, Cairo
items.description: A boutique Nile house of butler service and old-world calm, a notch quieter than the towers.

items.name: Waldorf Astoria Cairo Heliopolis
credentials: World Travel Awards, Egypt's Leading Business Hotel (2025)
items.description: Art-deco grandeur near the airport, the grand hotel for arrivals, departures and business.

items.name: Fairmont Nile City
items.description: A sleek modern Nile-front tower with a landmark rooftop pool over the river.

items.name: JW Marriott Hotel Cairo
credentials: World Travel Awards, Egypt's Leading Hotel Suite (2024)
World Travel Awards, Africa's Leading Conference Hotel (2024)
items.description: A resort-scaled Marriott on the city's eastern edge, golf, spa and space to spread out.

items.name: Conrad Cairo
credentials: World Travel Awards, Egypt's Leading Business Hotel (2024)
items.description: A dependable Nile-front business house, capable, central and easy on the bill.

items.name: The Pyramids of Giza & the Great Sphinx
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Memphis and its Necropolis / the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur
New7Wonders of the World, Great Pyramid of Giza
One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
items.description: The last surviving Wonder of the ancient world, and the one sight that hushes even seasoned travellers. Arrange a private Egyptologist and enter at opening, or before it, so the plateau is yours in the cool morning light rather than shared with the coach crowds and the midday heat. The interior of the Great Pyramid and the panorama point beyond the Sphinx are worth the extra tickets.

items.name: Dawn camel or Arabian-horse ride across the plateau
items.description: The most cinematic way to first see the pyramids, riding in from the desert side at sunrise, when the light is gold and the plateau is still empty. A good operator brings well-kept Arabian horses rather than the tired camels near the gate, and multi-generation families can go at a gentle walk. Photographers get the frame everyone wants before the crowds arrive.

items.name: Pyramids Sound & Light Show
items.description: After dark the Sphinx 'narrates' the story of the pyramids while lasers and coloured light play across the monuments, unashamedly theatrical, but a memorable evening for children and grandparents. Shows run nightly in rotating languages; a discreet private terrace or a nearby rooftop table lets you watch in comfort with dinner.

items.name: The Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM)
items.description: The largest archaeological museum in the world, opened in full in November 2025 beside the pyramids, and now the single most important museum visit in Egypt. The complete Tutankhamun collection is shown together for the first time since its discovery, and the vast atrium staircase of colossi is breathtaking. Entry is timed and online-only, book well ahead and take a private guide to make sense of 100,000 objects.

items.name: The Egyptian Museum, Tahrir Square
items.description: The grand old 1902 museum on Tahrir Square, still holding tens of thousands of masterpieces, Middle Kingdom, Late Period and Greco-Roman treasures, jewellery, papyri and coffins, even as Tutankhamun has moved to the GEM. The faded, cabinet-crammed halls have a scholarly romance the new museum can't replicate. Best paired with the GEM over two days, not one.

items.name: The National Museum of Egyptian Civilization (NMEC), the Royal Mummies
items.description: Home to the hushed, reverent Royal Mummies Hall, where 22 pharaohs and queens, Ramses II, Seti I, Hatshepsut among them, lie in a specially designed climate-controlled gallery. It is a genuinely moving, dignified experience rather than a spectacle. The wider museum traces Egyptian civilisation from prehistory to today, and is calm and rarely crowded.

items.name: The Citadel of Saladin & Mosque of Muhammad Ali
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: Saladin's 12th-century hilltop fortress crowned by the Ottoman-style alabaster Mosque of Muhammad Ali, whose silver domes and twin pencil minarets dominate the skyline. From the ramparts you look clear across the medieval city to the pyramids on a clear day. Go late afternoon for the light and cooler air; modest dress and slip-off shoes for the mosque.

items.name: Mosque-Madrasa of Sultan Hassan
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: The masterpiece of Mamluk architecture, a colossal 14th-century mosque and school whose soaring stone courtyard and towering iwan leave most visitors silent. It stands facing Al-Rifa'i across a small square, and the pair together is one of Cairo's great architectural set-pieces. A private guide unlocks the geometry and the history of the sultans buried within.

items.name: Al-Rifa'i Mosque
items.description: The younger neighbour of Sultan Hassan, completed in 1912 but built to echo Mamluk grandeur, and the royal mausoleum of Egypt's last kings, as well as the tomb of the last Shah of Iran. The marble-and-gilt interior is unexpectedly opulent. Visited together with Sultan Hassan on one ticket, it makes the finest hour of Islamic architecture in the city.

items.name: Al-Azhar Mosque
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: Founded in 970 AD, one of the oldest continuously operating universities in the world and the spiritual heart of Sunni Islam. The serene marble courtyard and layered minarets from different centuries reward a slow, quiet visit. It sits at the entrance to the old city, a natural start to a walk down Al-Muizz Street.

items.name: Mosque of Ibn Tulun
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: The oldest mosque in Cairo surviving in its original form, from 879 AD, vast, austere and almost empty, with a rare spiral minaret you can climb for a sweeping rooftop view over the old city. Its serene scale is a complete contrast to the bustle outside. Next door, the little Gayer-Anderson Museum occupies two restored merchant houses worth a look.

items.name: Al-Muizz Street
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: A pedestrianised open-air museum of medieval architecture, one of the densest concentrations of Islamic monuments anywhere, from the Qalawun complex to Bayt al-Suhaymi. Walk it in the evening when the sabils and minarets are floodlit and the heat has gone. A knowledgeable guide turns a beautiful stroll into a thousand years of history.

items.name: Khan el-Khalili bazaar
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: The great medieval souk, a warren of alleys selling silver, brass, lanterns, spices and perfume oils since the 14th century. Bargaining is expected and part of the theatre; a guide keeps the touts at bay and takes you to the honest workshops behind the tourist front. Pause for mint tea at the storied El Fishawy café, open more or less continuously for two centuries.

items.name: Al-Azhar Park
items.description: A gift of the Aga Khan built on what was five centuries of rubble, now a serene hilltop garden of formal terraces, fountains and a serpentine lake, with the finest panorama of every minaret in Islamic Cairo. The Citadel View restaurant at sunset is one of the loveliest tables in the city. A green, cooling pause in the middle of a dense day.

items.name: The Hanging Church (Al-Muallaqa)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: The most beloved of Cairo's ancient churches, suspended above a gatehouse of the Roman Babylon fortress, its nave seeming to float over the ruins. The dark wooden ceiling shaped like Noah's Ark and the inlaid pulpit are exquisite. The heart of the compact Coptic quarter, walkable in an easy morning.

items.name: Ben Ezra Synagogue
items.description: The oldest synagogue in Egypt, on a site linked by tradition to where the infant Moses was found, and famous among scholars for the Cairo Geniza, a treasury of a millennium of medieval manuscripts discovered in its loft. Small, atmospheric and beautifully restored. A poignant marker of Cairo's layered Jewish, Christian and Muslim history, all within a few steps.

items.name: The Coptic Museum
items.description: The world's finest collection of Coptic art, textiles, icons, carved wood and early Christian manuscripts, housed in a jewel-box building with mashrabiya screens and painted ceilings. Quieter and gentler than the pharaonic museums, and a revealing bridge between ancient Egypt and the Christian age. An hour here deepens the whole Coptic quarter.

items.name: Church of St Sergius (Abu Serga)
items.description: One of the oldest churches in Cairo, built over a crypt where tradition holds the Holy Family sheltered during their flight into Egypt. Simple, ancient and deeply venerated, it draws pilgrims as much as tourists. A short, meaningful stop on the Coptic circuit, especially for Christian travellers.

items.name: A Nile felucca at sunset
items.description: The oldest and most graceful way onto the river, a lateen-sailed felucca, chartered privately, drifting past Zamalek and the city skyline as the sun drops. No engine, no music, just the water and the light. The most peaceful hour in Cairo, and lovely for families or a quiet couple's evening.

items.name: A Nile dinner cruise
items.description: For an evening with more occasion, a dinner cruise glides past the illuminated city with dinner and, on the classic boats, a whirling-dervish tanoura show and belly dance. Choose a discreet premium operator or charter privately; ask ahead and the galley will happily lay on a full vegetarian or Jain menu. A crowd-pleaser across the generations.

items.name: Cairo Tower
items.description: The 187-metre lattice tower on Gezira Island, its openwork concrete inspired by a lotus stem, gives the best 360-degree view of the whole sprawl of Cairo and the Nile threading through it. Go for late afternoon and stay for the lights coming on. A quick, easy orientation for a first day in the city.

items.name: The galleries of Zamalek
items.description: Cairo's leafy island district is where the contemporary art scene lives, spaces like Gypsum, Ubuntu and the long-running Zamalek Art Gallery, alongside villa-lined streets, the Aisha Fahmy palace and good cafés. A civilised half-day for collectors and anyone wanting the modern city rather than the ancient one. Easily paired with lunch and a wander.

items.name: The Museum of Islamic Art
items.description: One of the greatest collections of Islamic art in the world, woodwork, metal, glass, ceramics and carpets spanning the whole Muslim world, beautifully re-displayed after restoration. Far less visited than the pharaonic museums, so it's calm and unhurried. Essential for anyone who falls for the artistry of Islamic Cairo and wants to understand it.

items.name: Manial Palace & Museum
items.description: The eccentric, gorgeous early-20th-century palace of Prince Mohamed Ali Tewfik, a magpie's mix of Ottoman, Moorish, Persian and Rococo set in a botanical garden on Rhoda Island. Gilded halls, tiled kilns and a throne room, and rarely crowded. A hidden gem for those who've done the headline sights and want something quieter and unexpectedly lavish.

items.name: The City of the Dead (Northern Cemetery)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: A vast living necropolis where centuries of Mamluk mausolea stand among a community that has made homes among the tombs, best seen respectfully and only with a sensitive local guide who has standing there. The soaring funerary complexes of Qaitbay and Barquq are architectural marvels. A profound, humane glimpse of a Cairo few visitors reach; never treat it as a spectacle.

items.name: A perfume-oil house visit
items.description: Egypt's essence trade goes back to the pharaohs, and a proper old atelier will sit you down with tiny bottles of jasmine, lotus, sandalwood and 'secret of the desert' over tea. A charming, low-pressure hour, buy the pure oils, skip the alcohol-based blends. Fun for the whole party, and a fragrant, packable gift to take home.

items.name: A papyrus-making demonstration
items.description: A short, genuine demonstration of how papyrus is beaten, soaked and pressed into a sheet, best at a reputable institute rather than a roadside shop, where the art is real and the paintings are hand-done on true papyrus, not banana leaf. Children love the hands-on part. A tasteful, authentic souvenir when you buy from the right place.

items.name: A carpet-and-textile workshop
items.description: On the road out to Saqqara, family carpet schools show children and weavers at the looms turning wool and silk into hand-knotted rugs and tapestries. It's a window into a craft as much as a shop, and a discreet guide will steer you to the honest houses with fair prices. Serious buyers can commission and ship.

items.name: Saqqara & the Step Pyramid of Djoser (day trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Memphis and its Necropolis / the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur
items.description: The world's oldest stone pyramid, Imhotep's revolutionary step pyramid of 2680 BC, anchoring a vast necropolis of painted tombs and the underground Serapeum with its colossal bull sarcophagi. Quieter and more atmospheric than Giza, and richer for a proper Egyptologist. The essential companion to the pyramids, half an hour south of the city.

items.name: Memphis, the ancient capital (day trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Memphis and its Necropolis / the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur
items.description: The capital of the Old Kingdom, now an open-air museum among the palm groves, its centrepiece a magnificent fallen colossus of Ramses II and a fine alabaster sphinx. Little remains standing, but it completes the story of Saqqara and Dahshur close by. A short, shaded stop, easily rolled into a single southern day.

items.name: Dahshur, the Bent & Red Pyramids (day trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Memphis and its Necropolis / the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur
items.description: Two of the most important pyramids in Egypt and among the least crowded: the Bent Pyramid, where the builders changed the angle mid-construction, and the Red Pyramid, the first true smooth-sided pyramid, which you can usually enter with barely another soul inside. Combined with Saqqara and Memphis, it is the finest pyramid day beyond Giza.

items.name: Alexandria (day trip)
items.description: Egypt's Mediterranean city and once the intellectual capital of the ancient world, the Corniche sea breeze, the strikingly modern Bibliotheca Alexandrina, the Roman catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa, Pompey's Pillar and Qaitbay Fort on the site of the ancient Pharos lighthouse. A long but rewarding day by car or the faster train, and a complete change of air from Cairo.

items.name: Wadi El Hitan, the Valley of the Whales (day trip)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Wadi Al-Hitan (Whale Valley)
items.description: A UNESCO-listed desert valley scattered with 40-million-year-old fossil skeletons of ancient whales, extraordinary evidence of evolution, set among sculpted sandstone in complete silence. It pairs with the lakes and waterfalls of Wadi El Rayan. A long drive best done as an overnight, or with a private 4x4 and picnic; a bucket-list day for curious families.

items.name: Fayoum Oasis, Tunis village & Lake Qarun (day trip)
items.description: A green oasis of waterwheels, olive groves and the ancient Lake Qarun, with the pottery village of Tunis on its shore, a cluster of artisan studios and pretty eco-lodges. A gentle, unhurried counterpoint to the monuments, good for slow lunches and buying ceramics. Best as a relaxed overnight from Cairo.

items.name: Wadi Degla Protectorate
items.description: A dramatic limestone canyon on the very edge of the city near leafy Maadi, laced with fossils and easy walking trails through the desert quiet, a genuine escape barely half an hour from downtown. Go early for the cool and the light. A refreshing morning of nature for those who want to stretch their legs between the museums.

items.name: Baron Empain Palace
items.description: A startling Hindu-temple-inspired mansion in the garden suburb of Heliopolis, built by a Belgian industrialist and long shrouded in ghost stories, now beautifully restored with a museum on the city's making. Its Angkor-and-Cambodia-styled towers are unlike anything else in Cairo. A quirky, elegant stop that intrigues Indian travellers in particular.

items.name: Bab Zuweila & the medieval gates
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: The great southern gate of Fatimid Cairo, from 1092, whose twin minarets you can climb for one of the finest close-up views over the roofs, domes and minarets of the old city. The Tentmakers' market (Khayamiya) with its hand-appliquéd fabrics runs just beside it. A rewarding climb and a living craft street, away from the main crush.

items.name: El Fishawy & the old cafés
items.description: El Fishawy, tucked in the lanes of Khan el-Khalili, has poured mint tea and shisha for some 250 years beneath its mirrored walls, a favourite of the Nobel laureate Naguib Mahfouz. Sit, watch the alley theatre, and let the sweet-tea sellers and rose-water hawkers come to you. The most atmospheric pause in the old city.

items.name: A whirling-dervish (tanoura) performance
items.description: The spinning Sufi tanoura at the restored Wikala of al-Ghuri is hypnotic, a spiritual dance of skirts and colour rather than a tourist floor-show, staged in a beautiful Mamluk caravanserai. Free or very low cost, and mesmerising for children. A gentle, uplifting evening in the heart of the medieval city.

items.name: Cairo food & street-food walk
items.description: Egyptian cooking is a joy for vegetarians, koshari (the beloved lentil-rice-pasta bowl), ful medames, taameya (Egyptian falafel of fava beans), fresh mango and sugar-cane juices. A private guide takes you to the best, cleanest tables and can arrange strictly veg or Jain-aware stops. Delicious, sociable, and revealing of the real Cairo.

items.name: A hot-air balloon is Luxor, instead, a helicopter or private-plane extension
items.description: For travellers with only days, a private-plane or fast-flight extension pairs Cairo with Luxor and Aswan, the temples of Karnak, the Valley of the Kings and a Nile dahabiya, without losing time to long drives. Your concierge sequences it as one seamless journey. The natural next chapter once Cairo's wonders are done.

items.name: Coptic & Islamic architecture photography walk
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Cairo
items.description: Cairo layers Roman, Coptic, Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman stone within a few square kilometres, a photographer's dream of mashrabiya screens, spiral minarets, painted ceilings and carved domes. A dawn walk with a guide who knows the light and the caretakers gets you inside courtyards before they open. Endlessly rewarding for anyone who loves buildings.

items.name: Gayer-Anderson Museum
items.description: Two joined 16th- and 17th-century merchant houses beside the Ibn Tulun mosque, filled by a British collector with Ottoman furniture, mashrabiya balconies and secret passages, a perfectly preserved window into old domestic Cairo (and a James Bond film set). Small, atmospheric and easily combined with the mosque next door. A charming hidden gem.

items.name: The Nilometer & Umm Kulthum Museum, Rhoda
items.description: At the southern tip of Rhoda Island, the elegant 9th-century Nilometer once measured the river's flood that decided Egypt's fortunes, beside a small museum to Umm Kulthum, the beloved 'Star of the East'. A quiet, offbeat pairing of ancient science and modern legend. A short, cultured stop for those who like the corners others miss.

items.name: Khufu's
credentials: MENA's 50 Best Restaurants No. 1 (2026), Best Restaurant in Egypt
The World's 50 Best Restaurants 2025, Resy One To Watch
items.description: Modern Egyptian cooking at the foot of the Great Pyramid, the finest table in the country, with the view to match.

items.name: Kazoku
items.description: Contemporary Japanese cooking with real precision, the city's most serious sushi and robata.

items.name: Sachi Cairo
items.description: Confident Mediterranean cooking, warm service and a proper wine list, a striking evening out.

items.name: Sachi Giza
items.description: The Giza-side Sachi, the same polished Mediterranean cooking, on the west bank.

items.name: Izakaya
items.description: A lively Japanese izakaya doing small plates and skewers with genuine intent.

items.name: Reif Kushiyaki Cairo
items.description: Charcoal-grilled Japanese skewers from the acclaimed kushiyaki name, small food, big flavour.

items.name: Zooba
items.description: Elevated Egyptian street food, koshary, ta'ameya and baladi bread, done with colour and real care.

items.name: The Roof, Four Seasons Cairo at Nile Plaza
credentials: Bar of a Forbes Four-Star / MICHELIN One-Key hotel (Four Seasons Cairo at Nile Plaza, 2025)
items.description: An open-air bar high above the Nile at the city's most exacting hotel, the drink with the finest river view.

items.name: The Rooftop, Kempinski Nile Hotel
credentials: Bar of a MICHELIN Guide hotel (Kempinski Nile Hotel, Cairo)
items.description: An eleventh-floor rooftop over the Nile and the skyline, a calm, grown-up nightcap above the city.

plan.heading: 4 days in Cairo, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Pyramids and Sphinx at opening with an Egyptologist, entering the Great Pyramid before the crowds.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Nine Pyramids Lounge facing the plateau, then rest at the Marriott Mena House garden.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at 139 Pavilion or Sachi Park St., with the pyramids lit in the distance.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A full private morning at the Grand Egyptian Museum, including the complete Tutankhamun collection.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Museum's Khufu solar boat and a late lunch on its terrace overlooking Giza.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A Nile-side dinner at the Four Seasons Nile Plaza, or Zooba's elevated Egyptian street food.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Sultan Hassan and Al-Rifa'i mosques, then the Citadel of Saladin for the view over the city.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Coptic Cairo, the Hanging Church and Ben Ezra Synagogue, then tea at El Fishawy in Khan el-Khalili.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Abou El Sid for classic Egyptian cooking, or Khufu's within the Al-Azhar Park gardens.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Egyptian Museum in Tahrir for the royal mummies, quieter now that Giza holds the crowds.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A slow felucca on the Nile at the golden hour, sailing between Zamalek and the city.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at the Nile Ritz-Carlton's Vivo, overlooking the river.

items.name: Zamalek
items.description: A leafy island in the Nile with embassies, galleries and quiet streets; the calmest, most civilised base in the city.

items.name: Giza / near the Pyramids
items.description: West of the river beside the plateau; suits those who want the Pyramids from their window and an early start on the site.

items.name: Garden City / Downtown
items.description: Faded belle-époque grandeur along the Nile; central and atmospheric for travellers who want to be in the thick of it.

events.name: Cairo International Film Festival
events.note: The oldest film festival in the Arab world and Africa, drawing an international crowd to the city's cinemas and red carpets.

events.name: Cairo Jazz Festival
events.note: A long-running gathering of Egyptian and international jazz musicians across the city's stages.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in Giza with a direct pyramid view or in Zamalek for calm; dress conservatively, and visit the plateau and the Grand Egyptian Museum early to beat both heat and crowds.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Cairo International (CAI); arrange a private chauffeur with meet-and-assist through immigration, as the visa-on-arrival and airport crowds are best handled by a fixer.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car and driver is non-negotiable in Cairo's dense traffic; a knowledgeable guide is invaluable at the pyramids and the Grand Egyptian Museum.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM works across the city; wifi in the better hotels is dependable, though speeds outside them can be modest.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Egyptian pound (EGP) is the currency; carry cash as many places prefer it, tip generously (baksheesh, roughly 10%) as it is woven into service culture.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October-April is the window, warm dry days, cool evenings, comfortable for the pyramids and the new Grand Egyptian Museum; May-September is punishingly hot, with 40°C-plus common in high summer.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: EgyptAir flies Delhi-Cairo nonstop (about 7 hours, limited weekly frequencies); otherwise a single Gulf stop on Emirates/Qatar/Etihad from Delhi or Mumbai. The Gulf routings give better cabins and lounges, use the Qatar Al Mourjan or Emirates lounge at the connecting hub.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Be current on hepatitis A and typhoid (both food/water-borne and a real risk here); routine vaccines too. Do not drink tap water or take ice, bottled only, and be careful with raw produce. Generally safe for the discreet traveller with a private guide/driver; ordinary care in crowds and against touts at sites.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Naturally vegetarian-friendly, ful, tameya (falafel), koshari, and vegetable tagines are staples; Jain workable with briefing. Indian food is available across upscale hotels; koshari itself is an easy, satisfying veg standby.
